title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler tests his lunar tables against a partial lunar eclipse. The tables give the node and the inclination; the observed duration of the eclipse is used to correct both. The unknowns are measured on the sphere from the ascending node: x is the arc along the ecliptic to the centre of the earth's shadow at mid-eclipse, y the arc along the lunar orbit to the moon's centre, and c = x − y.

End of §9. From the observed duration Euler has found 2x = −20°13'7", so x = −10°6'34". The tables gave x = −10°3'11". The true node therefore lies at 9s8°12'15" rather than 9s8°8'52", i.e. 3'23" further on. An earlier eclipse had already required an increase of 5'47". Euler concludes that the tabular node longitudes should be raised by a few minutes.

He then takes y − a = −10°30'6" and x − b = −10°8'23". These follow from y = x − c = −10°3'41", a = 26'25" and b = 1'49". He uses the half-angle form of the spherical law of cosines (written out on the next page). At first contact the triangle has its vertex at the node, legs x − b and y − a, included angle ρ, and opposite side f = α + β:
  sin²(ρ/2) = sin½(f − (c + a − b)) · sin½(f + (c + a − b)) / [sin(y − a) sin(x − b)].
Here c + a − b = 21'43", so the half-arcs are 19'22" and 41'5". He obtains log sin²(ρ/2) = 7.3218378 (tabular logs, characteristic +10), hence log sin(ρ/2) = 8.6609189. From this he reads ρ/2 = 2°37'21", ρ = 5°14'42", which is 1'47" smaller than the tabular 5°16'29".

§10, methodological critique. There are really three unknowns (x, ρ, c), but beginning and end of the eclipse give only two equations. Treating c as known is dangerous, because a small error in c produces large errors in x and ρ: the problem is ill-conditioned. The usual remedy for a partial eclipse is to add the magnitude of greatest obscuration, but that cannot be observed accurately. Euler therefore proposes total eclipses, where all four contacts (beginning, immersion, emersion, end) are observed. To avoid his complicated earlier formulas he will take three of these equations directly and solve for the unknowns.

§11, set-up.
- m and n are the hourly motions of sun and moon; k = 8" is the node's hourly (retrograde) motion.
- α is the shadow semidiameter and β the lunar semidiameter, with f = α + β and F = α − β.
- h is the time from beginning to end and H the time from immersion to emersion.
- a = ½h(n + k) and b = ½h(m + k) are the half-duration motions relative to the node; A and B are the same with H.
- The unknowns are x, y and ρ.
Each contact gives one spherical-cosine relation:
  cos ρ = [cos f − cos(y ∓ a) cos(x ∓ b)] / [sin(y ∓ a) sin(x ∓ b)], and likewise with F, A, B.
That is four expressions for one cos ρ, with three unknowns. On the next page Euler drops one equation and solves the remaining two equalities for the corrections to x and y. He does this by a two-variable 'regula falsi' with three trial hypotheses, in effect a bivariate secant / linear-interpolation method.
errors: Probable arithmetic slip converting the logarithm to an angle. The log itself checks: recomputing sin(19'22")·sin(41'5")/[sin(10°30'6")·sin(10°8'23")] gives sin²(ρ/2) ≈ 2.098×10⁻³, i.e. log ≈ 7.32186, matching Euler's 7.3218378. Half of that is 8.6609189, so sin(ρ/2) ≈ 0.045806, which corresponds to ρ/2 ≈ 2°37'31", not 2°37'21". Then ρ ≈ 5°15'2", and the deficit from the tables would be about 1'27" rather than 1'47". (This assumes the printed '21' is not a misprint for '31'; the internal consistency ρ = 2×2°37'21" = 5°14'42" suggests Euler himself used 21".)

Minor point: the formulas as written treat the shadow and moon motions along the ecliptic and orbit as if measured from a fixed node, with k added to both motions. This is standard and consistent, not an error.

ideas.what: Correcting the tabular node longitude and orbital inclination from the observed times of an eclipse, using spherical triangles at the node
ideas.modern_name: Determination of orbital elements from eclipse contact timings (differential correction of lunar tables)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical practice (Halley, Mayer, Euler and others in the 18th century)
ideas.where_published: Euler's lunar-theory writings; this particular piece printed posthumously (E838, Opera postuma 1862)

ideas.what: Recognition that two contact equations cannot fix three unknowns, and that a small error in the assumed c produces large errors in x and ρ
ideas.modern_name: Underdetermination / ill-conditioning (sensitivity) of a parameter estimation problem
ideas.usually_credited_to: General astronomical practice; formalized later in error theory

ideas.what: Using all four contacts of a total eclipse in place of the poorly observable magnitude of greatest obscuration
ideas.modern_name: Choice of better-conditioned observables (contact timings of total eclipses)

ideas.what: Solving two coupled transcendental equations for two corrections by three trial hypotheses (announced here, executed on the next page)
ideas.modern_name: Multivariate regula falsi / secant method (interpolating a plane through three trial points)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Generalized false position, known in astronomical computation in the 18th century; the multivariate secant is formalized much later

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine applied-astronomy computation and a sensible methodological remark. The bivariate regula falsi is mildly interesting but is standard computational practice of the period. The only new observation is a probable 10" slip in converting the logarithm to an angle.
transcription_corrections: Line 5: '$x = -10^0 30' 6''$' should read '$y - a = -10^0 30' 6''$'. The value follows from y = x − c = −10°3'41" and a = 26'25".
Line 6: '$\frac{1}{2}\varrho = 8,6609189$' should be '$l\sin\frac{1}{2}\varrho = 8,6609189$', a logarithm of the sine.
Line 1: the start is likely 'Ergo longitudo nodi vera...'. Line 2: 'scilicet 3'23" promotior esse debebat'.
Before the second pair of cos ρ formulas, 'longque' is probably 'itemque' (or 'atque'), partly illegible in the scan.
In §11 the scan reads 'ponaturque' and 'Tum sint incognitae quantitates', matching the transcription.
